sources.passagesActuallyRead: Market orders do not guarantee an execution price; last-traded price may differ. Limit orders set a price boundary; a stop order becomes a market order on its trigger.
Equal amounts at regular intervals buy more units when prices are lower and fewer when higher.

Investments involve uncertainty and potential financial loss. The selected page describes business, volatility, inflation, interest-rate and liquidity risks; it does not define Calmar or validate a strategy.

routes.assessment: The equal-contribution explanation is corroborated by the actual SEC DCA definition. Fee-free $100 at $10 plus $100 at $20 buys 15 units at $200/15, about $13.33; the falling-price worksheet buys 30 units at $200/30, about $6.67, but a $5 mark gives $150 and a $50 loss. Lower average cost is explicitly distinguished from profit and lump-sum outperformance. The body, summary and worksheet repeat core concepts but the adverse-path worksheet adds a useful distinct example; no entire after-footer article repetition. Broader cross-site originality and complete source fit remain.

$100 to $80 is a 20% peak decline and 25% recovery on the lower base; a 50% loss requires 100% recovery. Cash flows, sampling, unfinished decline, historical versus future bounds and lack of health diagnosis are explicit. The SEC risk reference is correctly labelled background; it does not establish the Calmar ratio definition or all drawdown conventions. Those claim-specific source follow-ups remain. Compared with the lesson on handling drawdowns, the shared arithmetic illustrates the same concept; this page adds unfinished maximum-drawdown sampling and Calmar scope, without enough evidence to assert improper duplication.

The 1:1, 1:2 and 1:3 fixed realised payoff examples break even before costs at 1/2, 1/3 and 1/4 wins respectively. 0.25 times $3 minus 0.75 times $1 is zero; a positive per-trade cost makes it negative. Planned targets and stops do not establish realised payoff sizes, frequencies or positive expectancy. Actual SEC source text supports market-price uncertainty and stop-to-market conversion, not profitability, a universal ratio or strategy validation. Broader source/originality and complete conditional/accessibility stages remain.

The worksheet ten units at $20 plus 0.1% costs debits $200.20, selling at $19 less 0.1% credits $189.81 and loses $10.39. A separate $20 to $18 mark loses $20 before costs. These are hypothetical arithmetic, not live execution tests. The text distinguishes virtual funds/generated histories from queue priority, real slippage, limit orders, borrowing, settlement and real-money readiness. SEC order mechanics provides selected execution background, not certification of the simulator engine or a measured psychological claim. No production trade or private-account action was performed.
